earnings_text.text: Fiscal Q4 2026 (July 29, 2026): revenue $90.0 billion vs $87.6 billion expected, EPS $4.74 vs $4.24 expected, Azure up 43% in constant currency vs 40% the prior quarter. Stock rose 8% because management raised capex plans and cited demand. Fiscal Q3 2026 (April) showed the same pattern: beat, higher capex, mixed reaction. The debate is entirely about whether $190 billion of capex earns a return, not about current demand.

read.prior_quarter_label: Fiscal Q3 2026 (April; exact report date not stated)
read.headline: Microsoft beat on both revenue and EPS with Azure accelerating to 43% in constant currency, and management answered by raising capex plans rather than easing spend, which the stock rewarded with an 8% move.

guidance.detail: The single management action the note records at the Q4 FY2026 print is a raise to capex plans, paired with a demand citation, and the stock rose 8% on it. The note attaches no dollar amount, no period, and no prior baseline to the raise, so its size cannot be read from the source. The word 'guidance' does not appear anywhere in the note.
guidance.quote: Stock rose 8% because management raised capex plans and cited demand.

guidance.what: Scale of the capex program (~$190 billion, up 61%)
guidance.detail: Corrected from a prior version that labeled this a raise. The note states this figure inside the bear-case section as a spending level and growth rate. It is not described as guidance, not attributed to management, and not dated to the Q4 report, so no guidance action can be attached to it. It is also not reconciled against the separate 'capex rose 70% to $41 billion for the fiscal year' figure in the business-quality section.
guidance.quote: Microsoft is spending roughly $190 billion on capex, up 61%, and depreciation will weigh on reported earnings for years.

tone.assessment: Leaning in rather than defensive. The note portrays management as answering a beat by committing more capital and pointing at demand, and the market taking that as confidence rather than as overreach. The note also frames the argument as settled on demand and open only on returns, which is consistent with a management posture that is confident on the top line.
tone.evidence: Stock rose 8% because management raised capex plans and cited demand.
tone.confidence: low. The note contains no direct management quotes, no prepared-remarks or Q&A content, and no call transcript. This read rests on one sentence of secondary summary plus the note author's framing of the debate. Tone in the sense of how management actually sounded is not observable from this source.

new_risks.risk: Depreciation from the capex build weighing on reported earnings for years. The note does not mark this as new this quarter; it is a standing bear-case item.
new_risks.quote: Microsoft is spending roughly $190 billion on capex, up 61%, and depreciation will weigh on reported earnings for years.

new_risks.risk: OpenAI concentration in the commercial backlog plus OpenAI investment losses flowing through the income statement. OpenAI restructuring that reduces committed Azure spend is separately named as a thesis killer.
new_risks.quote: Forty five percent of the $625 billion commercial backlog is tied to OpenAI, and OpenAI investment losses ($3.1 billion in one quarter) flow through Microsoft's income statement.

new_risks.risk: Free cash flow compression as capex scales. Stated in the business-quality section rather than the bear case, but the underlying risk (sub-20% full-year free cash flow margin) is a named thesis killer. The note does not identify which quarter the $15.8 billion figure covers.
new_risks.quote: Free cash flow fell to $15.8 billion in a recent quarter from $20.3 billion a year earlier as capex rose 70% to $41 billion for the fiscal year.

new_risks.risk: Copilot losing seat share to cheaper agents on branding and interoperability grounds.
new_risks.quote: Copilot has had branding and interoperability complaints and could lose seat share to cheaper agents.

new_risks.risk: Revenue deceleration against a fixed cost base if AI demand slows or hyperscaler pricing turns competitive.
new_risks.quote: If AI demand slows or hyperscaler pricing gets competitive, revenue decelerates while costs keep growing.

new_risks.risk: Negligible insider ownership. Stated in the business-quality section and not carried into the bear case or the thesis killers.
new_risks.quote: Insider ownership is negligible; management's track record on cloud is the best in large cap tech.

dodged.topic: What the ~$190 billion capex program actually returns, and over what horizon
dodged.reasoning: The note names this as the whole of the open argument ('The debate is entirely about whether $190 billion of capex earns a return, not about current demand') and records no management answer to it. The only management response the note captures is raising capex plans and citing demand, which addresses demand, the part the note says is not in dispute, and not returns, the part that is. Caveat on confidence: this is a secondary research note, not a transcript, so an unrecorded answer and a dodged question look identical here.

dodged.topic: OpenAI concentration and the earnings drag from OpenAI investment losses
dodged.reasoning: The note carries hard numbers on the exposure (45% of a $625 billion backlog, $3.1 billion of investment losses in one quarter) and names OpenAI restructuring as a thesis killer, yet records no management framing, contract duration, or mitigation anywhere in the earnings section. A concentration that large drawing no recorded commentary at the print is conspicuous, though again the note may simply not have preserved it.

dodged.topic: Free cash flow trajectory as capex scales
dodged.reasoning: The note reports free cash flow falling to $15.8 billion from $20.3 billion with capex up 70%, and separately makes a sub-20% full-year free cash flow margin a thesis killer, but attaches no management explanation, no forward free cash flow frame, and no identification of which quarter the decline belongs to. The metric closest to a stated break condition is the one with the least recorded commentary.

dodged.topic: Copilot monetization: seat counts, pricing, attach rates
dodged.reasoning: The note raises branding and interoperability complaints and a seat-share threat, and the bear case contemplates Copilot seats consolidating, but no seat, pricing, or attach figures appear anywhere in the note despite Copilot being called the company's biggest AI distribution channel. Lower confidence: a research note of this length may omit segment detail for space rather than because it was withheld.

dodged.topic: The depreciation schedule implied by the capex build
dodged.reasoning: The bear case asserts depreciation 'will weigh on reported earnings for years' with no quantification, no timing, and no management-provided schedule recorded. The note treats the drag as directional only. Lower confidence for the same transcript-absence reason.

not_determinable: Forward guidance of any kind. The note contains no revenue, EPS, margin, or Azure growth guide for Q1 FY2027 or FY2027, and the words 'guidance', 'guided', and 'outlook' do not appear in the file at all.

The size of the capex raise. The note says capex plans were raised but gives no figure, period, or prior baseline. Whether the ~$190 billion bear-case number is the raised plan, a multi-year aggregate, or a different measure entirely cannot be determined from the note.

Reconciliation of the two capex figures. 'capex rose 70% to $41 billion for the fiscal year' (business quality) and 'roughly $190 billion on capex, up 61%' (bear case) are never reconciled; the note does not state whether they differ by period, scope, or definition.

What management actually said. The note is a secondary summary with no direct quotes, no prepared remarks, and no Q&A, so questions asked, answers given, and anything genuinely evaded on the call are all outside the source. Every 'dodged' item above is an inference from absence in this note, not an observed non-answer.
Segment detail. No Intelligent Cloud, Productivity and Business Processes, or More Personal Computing revenue or margin splits appear. Only Azure growth rates are given.
Which quarter the free cash flow figures cover. The note says '$15.8 billion in a recent quarter from $20.3 billion a year earlier' without naming the quarter, so it cannot be tied to Q4 FY2026.

Capital returns. The note contains no dividend, buyback, or repurchase disclosure. Diluted share count is given annually only, 7,472m in FY2023 to 7,453m in FY2026 (a prior version of this extraction stated 'about 0.2% a year of shrinkage'; that figure was wrong and is withdrawn. The table's total move is roughly a quarter of one percent across three years). With no repurchase dollars and no authorization, the buyback program cannot be characterized from this note.

Estimate revision detail. The note's only revision datum is 'Next fiscal year EPS estimate moved +4.2% in 90 days.' There is no analyst count, no up-versus-down revision breakdown, no 30-day window, and no FY1-versus-FY2 split anywhere in the note. A prior version of this extraction cited a '+4.18% on FY1, with 19 upward and 4 downward revisions in 30 days' as corroboration; those numbers are not in this file and that claim is withdrawn.

Whether any risk is new this quarter. The note presents the bear-case and thesis-killer items as standing positions and does not date any of them to the Q4 print, so 'new' cannot be established from the source.

Consensus beyond two Q4 lines. Only Q4 revenue ($87.6 billion expected) and EPS ($4.24 expected) consensus are given. There is no Azure consensus, no segment consensus, and no forward-quarter consensus.
Q3 FY2026 specifics. That quarter is characterized only as 'beat, higher capex, mixed reaction', with no revenue, EPS, or Azure figures.
The price path after the print. The note gives an 8% reaction on July 29, 2026 and a price of $510.12 on 2026-09-04, with nothing in between, so whether the 8% move held cannot be determined.

Any position, journal entry, or prior wrong-if conditions. A prior version of this extraction compared the note's thesis killers against a logged journal 'wrong-if'; the word 'journal' does not appear in this file, and no position sizing, entry price, or cost basis appears either. That comparison drew on a separate document, is out of scope for a single-note extraction, and is withdrawn. Within this note, all four break conditions sit together in one 'Key risks and thesis killers' section: Azure under 30% with capex rising, OpenAI restructuring cutting committed Azure spend, full-year free cash flow margin under 20%, and a close under $400.
Balance sheet and cost detail. No stock-based compensation, headcount, tax rate, interest expense, or quarterly balance-sheet data. Net debt is annual only.
History before FY2023. The note states 'Four fiscal years is all the source provides.'

Data vintage. All screen and statement data is pulled 2026-09-04, roughly five weeks after the July 29 print, so nothing in the note reflects developments after that date. Next earnings is stated as 2026-10-28.
read.market_reaction: The stock rose 8% on the Q4 FY2026 print, which the note attributes to management raising capex plans and citing demand ("Stock rose 8% because management raised capex plans and cited demand."). The prior quarter produced a different outcome on the same setup: "Fiscal Q3 2026 (April) showed the same pattern: beat, higher capex, mixed reaction." As of the 2026-09-04 data pull the stock was $510.12, described as -10% from its 52 week high and -8% from its all time high, with forward P/E of 21.6 against a four year median of 35.8. The note gives no closing prices between July 29 and September 4, so whether the 8% move held, faded, or extended is not determinable from this source.

read.standing_caveat: A research note is already a summary, so its silence is usually the author compressing rather than management evading. Every entry under 'not addressed' below should be read at the confidence it states, and none of them is evidence about what was said on the call, because no transcript was available. See NOTES.md.

thesis.why_on_the_list: Compounder bucket. Rank 15 on quality. Forward P/E of 21.6 against a four year median of 35.8, the lowest multiple in three years, with Azure growth accelerating to 43% in the June quarter. The stock is only 8% off its high, so this is a quality at fair price idea, not a bargain.
thesis.business_quality: Distribution moat: Microsoft 365 is the default in most enterprises, Azure is one of three hyperscalers, and the company owns the biggest AI distribution channel through Copilot. Fiscal 2026 Azure revenue passed $100 billion, up 41%. Free cash flow fell to $15.8 billion in a recent quarter from $20.3 billion a year earlier as capex rose 70% to $41 billion for the fiscal year. Insider ownership is negligible; management's track record on cloud is the best in large cap tech.
thesis.verdict: Buy, in the October tranche. Buy zone $465 to $525. Conviction 4 of 5.

logged.thesis: Azure accelerating to 43%, fiscal Q4 beat on both lines, lowest multiple in three years at 21.6x forward. Quality at a fair price rather than a bargain.
logged.wrong_if: Azure growth under 30% with capex still rising, or a close under $400.

risks.bear_case: Microsoft is spending roughly $190 billion on capex, up 61%, and depreciation will weigh on reported earnings for years. Forty five percent of the $625 billion commercial backlog is tied to OpenAI, and OpenAI investment losses ($3.1 billion in one quarter) flow through Microsoft's income statement. If AI demand slows or hyperscaler pricing gets competitive, revenue decelerates while costs keep growing. Copilot has had branding and interoperability complaints and could lose seat share to cheaper agents. A 2026 bear target of $340 assumes the multiple stays compressed while free cash flow stays messy.
killers: Azure growth under 30% while capex keeps rising, OpenAI restructuring that reduces committed Azure spend, or free cash flow margin under 20% for a full year

wrong_if.text: Azure growth under 30% with capex still rising, or a close under $400.

multiples.label: Forward P/E
multiples.basis_note: The two sides are not the same multiple. The left is a forward P/E, the Street's estimate of next year's earnings. The median on the right is trailing: the price at each fiscal year end divided by that year's reported diluted EPS. Where earnings are expected to grow, forward is mechanically lower than trailing, so this column reads cheap by construction.

multiples.label: EV/EBITDA
multiples.basis_note: Both sides are trailing, so this comparison is like for like.

own_history.caveat: The median is taken at 4 fiscal year ends, so it is a 4-point median. That is a thin basis for 'cheap against its own history' and it says nothing about whether the old multiple was deserved.
own_history.basis_warning: Read the P/E row with care. Across the 138 names that carry both comparisons, 85% print a negative 'vs median' on forward P/E with a median of -29%, against 51% and -0.6% on EV/EBITDA where both sides are trailing. That gap is the basis mismatch, not 138 companies being cheap. It is also correlated with growth: faster-growing names look cheaper here (rank correlation -0.28 against revenue CAGR, versus -0.16 for EV/EBITDA), because their forward earnings are further above their trailing ones. The score weights the like-for-like EV/EBITDA comparison more heavily for exactly this reason.

drawdown.caveat: The all-time high is the highest closing price; the 52-week high is an intraday high. They are not on the same basis, and the drawdown from the all-time high is therefore understated.

price_basis.note: The drawdowns and the multiple-versus-median above were computed inside the price screen from its own last close, which is not quite the price shown at the top of this page: the two come from different passes of the pipeline and differ by a fraction of a percent. Neither is wrong; they are just not the same number.

peers.reasoning: Neither its multiple nor its quality separates it from its peers, and the two are close to each other. Most of the list is here, and that is the honest answer for most of the list.
peers.why: The own-history comparison above says nothing about whether the old multiple was deserved. This asks a different question: where does this name sit among its peers on price, and where does it sit among them on the things a price is supposed to reflect.

written_view.text: At $510 and 21.6x forward earnings the stock is well below its own 35.8x median and below Alphabet (23x) despite faster cloud growth. Three year view: if EPS compounds 13% a year the stock reaches roughly $34 of EPS in fiscal 2029. Bear: 20x on $30 (capex crushes free cash flow, Copilot seats consolidate) is $600, modest upside because the starting multiple is already low. Base: 26x on $34 is $880. Bull: 30x on $36 is $1,080.

score.caveat: A percentile against 150 names on one date. It has not been backtested; see the positioning page for why not.
